claims.text: A controlled, modest increase in phosphorus content will improve glass-forming ability in phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
A controlled, modest increase in phosphorus content will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
Extra phosphorus strengthens short-range atomic order.
Extra phosphorus increases atomic packing density.
The phosphorus-induced change in short-range atomic arrangement raises the energy barrier for nucleation of crystalline phases.
The phosphorus-induced change in short-range atomic arrangement raises the energy barrier for growth of crystalline phases.
The increased energy barrier retards crystallization during alloy processing.
The increased energy barrier retards crystallization during subsequent thermal exposure.
An alloy with increased phosphorus should have a lower critical cooling rate than an otherwise comparable lower-phosphorus baseline.
An alloy with increased phosphorus should have a higher crystallization onset temperature than an otherwise comparable lower-phosphorus baseline.
The intervention is expected to work under typical rapid-cooling or other processing conditions used to form amorphous alloys.
Excessively high processing temperature may diminish the beneficial effect of increased phosphorus.
An inappropriate balance between phosphorus and the other alloying elements may prevent the predicted improvement.
Approaching other phase boundaries may prevent the increased-phosphorus alloy from showing the predicted benefits.

contradictions.description: Increasing the phosphorus concentration while keeping every other element concentration constant is impossible for a normalized composition such as atomic percent: increasing the phosphorus fraction necessarily decreases at least one other elemental fraction. The intended constraint may instead be constant relative ratios or constant absolute amounts of the other elements.
